topics.title: Give Your Gate an Over-Refusal Budget
topics.dek: Safety that blocks billing questions is not safety—it is product damage. Track false refusals with the same seriousness as jailbreaks.

sections.heading: Two failure modes, one scoreboard
paragraphs: Most red-team suites optimize for under-refusal (harmful asks that succeed). Production users feel over-refusal first: legitimate refund, password-reset, or policy questions that get a blanket no.
Split your weekly scoreboard: jailbreak fail rate and over-refusal rate on a fixed set of legitimate intents. Ship only if both stay under agreed thresholds.

sections.heading: Build the legitimate set
sections.body: Collect twenty real support or product intents that must work. Tag each with expected tool use. Score with a simple rubric: appropriate_refusal, over_refusal, compliant. LLM-as-judge is fine if a human spot-checks ten percent.

sections.heading: When over-refusal spikes
sections.body: Do not loosen every guardrail globally. Diff the last system-prompt or filter change, replay the legitimate set, and restore the previous prompt if the safety set is still green. Treat over-refusal regressions like availability incidents.

topics.title: Put Red-Team Findings in the Sprint Backlog—Not the Slack Graveyard
topics.dek: A finding without a ticket, severity, and retest owner will return in the next release. Here is a lightweight intake that QA can run in under thirty minutes.

sections.heading: Intake fields that matter
paragraphs: For each finding capture: attack family, repro prompt, observed vs expected behavior, span or log evidence link, severity (blocker / major / minor), and the release train it blocks.
Map severity to policy: blockers stop the train, majors need a dated waiver with an executive owner, minors enter the next sprint with a named fixer.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.body: No finding is done until the repro prompt is in the regression suite and fails closed on main. The ticket description should link that prompt id. Otherwise you are collecting stories, not reducing risk.

sections.heading: Cadence
sections.body: Fifteen-minute triage after each red-team session; thirty-minute review in sprint planning. Keep a running count of open blockers on the QA dashboard next to flake rate.

topics.title: Shadow Your Safety Gate on Production Traffic Before You Enforce It
topics.dek: Flipping a new evaluator to blocking without a shadow week creates false confidence—or false outages. Run dark for seven days first.

sections.heading: What shadow mode means
sections.body: Score live or sampled traces with the new evaluator, write results to your observability store, and page nobody. Compare against the current gate. You want precision and recall estimates before you fail builds.

sections.heading: Exit criteria
paragraphs: After seven days: false-positive rate under your agreed budget on sampled human review, no unexplained spike correlated with a single customer segment, and at least one true positive that your old gate missed.
Only then flip the evaluator to blocking in CI or pre-prod. Keep a kill switch owned by the incident commander.

sections.heading: QA's job in the shadow week
sections.body: Sample twenty scored traces daily, label them, and publish a one-pager. If labels disagree with the evaluator more than ten percent, fix the rubric before enforcement.
